listenings.text: People assume the difficult part is the research. It is not. The difficult part is the first sentence, because the first sentence has to decide what the life was about, and it has to do it in one line, before anybody has read anything else. Get that wrong and the other nine hundred words are an argument with your own opening. The best ones to write, by a long way, are the people nobody has heard of. A woman who ran the same shop for fifty-one years. A man who kept the records of a football club that no longer exists. You have no template, so you have to find out what the life actually was. And there is one sentence I have never written and never will. I do not write that somebody lost a battle with an illness. Nobody loses a battle by dying. It was never a battle and they never agreed to fight it.

I want to make an objection to the whole form, and I should say at the start that I read biographies constantly and enjoy them enormously, so take this as a family argument. My objection is this. A biography imposes a shape that nobody had while they were living. Look at the grammar and you can watch it happening. He was to become. She was never to see. Those forms are only available to somebody standing at the end of the story, and every time one appears, a decision has been taken about what mattered, on evidence the subject never had. The years that look like a prologue were not a prologue to the person living them. They were eleven years, and they were the whole of their thirties, and at no point did anybody feel that they were waiting for the letter from Bologna.

extra_audio.text: Marta says the hardest part is deciding on page one what the life was for. He points out that every sentence is written by somebody who already knows the ending. She agrees, and shows how the grammar gives the writer away. He asks how she wrote the decade the subject never mentioned. She admits that her first draft turned ten real years into a prologue.

paras: The obituary ran to nine hundred words and the first sentence called her the founder of a school of thought. She would have disliked the phrase. She had spent forty years insisting that there was no school, that the people described as her followers disagreed with her about everything important, and that a body of work is not a movement. The obituary was accurate about the facts and wrong about the person, which is the usual outcome.

She was fifty-three before she hit her stride. Before that there had been an apprenticeship of twelve years, two false starts in a field she left without explanation, and a long period of obscurity during which she published almost nothing. She was self-taught in the subject that made her name, and she was to remain slightly defensive about it for the rest of her life.

The middle of the story is the part biographers find difficult. She fell out of favor in her sixties, comprehensively and in public, and she was overshadowed for a decade by a former protege who had been her most careful reader. She was about to withdraw the second volume when the institute in Bologna wrote to her. She would go on to spend eleven years there, produce the work everybody now cites, and never once mention the decade in between.

What survives is not what she expected. The books have dated; the argument she thought was her lasting legacy is now taught as a stage that the field passed through. The school she said did not exist has three hundred members. And a short paper she wrote in a fortnight, which she considered a distraction, was to be vindicated thirty years later by evidence she was never to see.
